en: *Śrautapadārthanirvacanam*: Either Indra or Mahendra is prescribed as the deity. Although the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is the substance [for the offering], two additional substances are prescribed there: one is milk and the second is curd. Because he brings these two together for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*), such a sacrificer is designated as *sannayan*, based on the verbal root *sī* (to bring together). Furthermore, by the rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the sūtra *pāyasānnāyye*, the terms *dadhi* and *payas* are denoted by the word *sānnāyya* through a derivation based on the object (*karman*).

If, due to incapacity, the number of cows for preparing the *sānnāyya* and the curd-milk (*dadhi-payas*) is made fewer than required, it must not be less than six; that is, one should not employ fewer than six cows. If more than six are desired, that is perfectly acceptable. The ritual separation of the calves from these cows by means of the previously invoked branch, accompanied by a mantra, is called *vatsāpākaraṇa* (the driving away of the calves).

Then, having cut the leaves from that branch and having cut a portion of the base measuring a span (prādeśa), he fashions it into the shape of a poker (dhṛṣṭi); this is called the *upaveṣa*, which is used at the time of preparing the *unnāyya* offering for the purpose of pushing out the embers of the Gārhapatya fire toward the north and other such functions.
The upper portion, however, bound in the shape of three braided strands of darbha grass, is designated by the term *śākhāpavitra*; its utility is in the evening milking and other such rites.

In the case of a sacrificer who has not prepared the sacrificial fires, since there is no fetching of the branch, the Adhvaryu, immediately after the commencement of the vow (*vratopāyana*), takes up from the north of the Gārhapatya fire an *asida* (a small axe) or a dog’s hatchet with the mantra. An *asida* is defined as a razor made of iron used for cutting.
Thus, an axe suitable for cutting sacrificial grass and other such tasks is called a "dog's axe" (*śvaparaśu*), because it is like a dog.

Having taken one of those two [blades], he goes to the place of the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra; having looked at the altar (vedi) with the mantra, he goes to the place for the Darbha grass and grasps a handful of Darbha sufficient for the *prastara*. "Grasping" (*parigrahaṇa*) refers to the circling [of the blade] around the entire Darbha-handful that is to be cut, using a knife or similar tool, in order to separate it.

When the handful of *darbha* grass is cut, that portion of the root which remains visible on the ground is designated by the word "cutting" (*chedana*) because it serves as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the action of cutting; this is indicated by the suffix *lyuṭ*.

According to the scriptural injunction, "In cases of cutting, piercing, digging, rites for the ancestors (*paitṛka*), rites for the *rākṣasa*, rites for Rudra (*raudra*), and malevolent spells (*abhicāraṇīya*), there shall be the consecration of water," the washing of the right hand with water prescribed for the sake of purification after performing acts such as cutting, piercing, digging, ancestral rites, *rākṣasa* rites, *raudra* rites, and malevolent spells is called "touching water" (*udakopasparśana*).

In that regard, during the *prakṛti-iṣṭi*, four handfuls of *darbha* grass are cut. The first handful of *darbha* is consecrated with mantras; it is placed upon the altar as the *juhū* [ladle], and above two *darbha* blades known as the *vidhṛti*, which point northward, that which is placed pointing eastward is called the *prastara*. The other three handfuls are accomplished solely through ritual actions without mantras; they are for the purpose of spreading over the altar and are fit for placing the vessels of the oblations, being designated by the term *barhis*.

Taking three blades of *darbha* grass and winding them clockwise, one joins another set of three *darbha* blades at their tips with the roots [of the first set] and makes them appear as if tied by the winding. Having wound that [second set] in the same manner, one does the same again with another three *darbha* blades at its tip; when this is done, three joints are formed in the middle. Having doubled that *darbha* cord, a knot should be made at the end. With this, the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is bound;
therefore, this is called the "binding of the sacrificial grass" (*barhiḥ-saṃnahanam*), also known as the "rope" (*śulba*).

Thus, for the purpose of binding the fuel, there is that which is called the *idhmasaṃnahana* (the cord for binding the fuel), also known by the name *śulba*. After the gathering of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the Adhvaryu goes to the place of the fuel and cuts the fuel with a knife or a small axe, silently. In it, there are twenty-one pieces of wood. Among them, three pieces of wood are for the purpose of placing them upon the first girdle to the south, north, and west of the Āhavanīya fire; they are equal in length to the girdle because they are placed all around the Āhavanīya. [He places] the sun in front mentally.
Because they are conceived as enclosures, they are designated as *paridhis*.

The other pieces of wood are each a span (*prādeśa*) long; among them, fifteen are for the purpose of the *sāmidhenī* verses, one is for the purpose of the *anuyāja* offerings, and two are for the purpose of being planted upright with their tips pointing upward in the southern and northern portions of the *āhavanīya* hearth-site. These eighteen pieces of wood are what are denoted by the term *samidh*.

In certain modified sacrifices (*vikṛti-iṣṭi*) and the like, even additional *samidh* fuel-sticks are included when there is an increase in the *sāmidhenī* verses; thus, a collection of twenty-one pieces of wood is denoted by the term *idhma*.
At the time of cutting the *idhma*, those small fragments of wood that fall here and there are designated by the term *idhmapravraścana*, derived from the sense of "instrument" (*karaṇa*).

The well-cooked rice, sufficient for the meal of even the four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), which is brought in after the sacrifice—subsequently, that is, following the ritual—for the purpose of feeding the priests, is designated by the term *anvāhārya* according to its etymological derivation (*karmavyutpatti*) as "that which is brought in subsequently."
The vessel in which the *anvāhārya* rice is cooked is called the *anvāhāryasthālī*.
The vessel in which the boiling waters (madantī) are heated is itself also designated by the term "boiling waters" (madantī).

Having threshed the rice and other grains related to the *puroḍāśa* and *caru* offerings with a pestle in a mortar, one performs the *phalīkaraṇa*—the process of removing the husks—using a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*). Those husks and other particles that fall away during this process are designated by the term *phalīkaraṇa*, derived from the sense of the action itself (*karaṇa*-vyutpatti). After the sacrifice, their oblation (*homa*) is prescribed to be performed in the *dakṣiṇāgni* fire along with four spoonfuls (*caturgṛhīta*) of clarified butter (*ājya*) using a ladle (*juhū*). Therefore, the vessel made of *aśvattha* wood constructed for keeping them until the completion of the sacrifice is called the *phalīkaraṇapātra*.

When the Adhvaryu priest proceeds with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings at the Gārhapatya fire, then—at the time of the sacrifice to the wives of the gods—for the purpose of receiving their share of the oblation from the wives of the gods who have arrived, there is a screen made of Aśvattha wood; because it is shaped like a mat and is suitable for concealment due to the modesty arising from their femininity, it is called an *antardhānakaṭa*.

After entering the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), the *adhvaryu* sits to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire, performs the *iḍājapa*, and recites the verse beginning with "devā gātuvid. Because the word "vāta" (wind) occurs in that verse—and because in the Śruti the word "vāta" is used to describe both the commencement and the conclusion of a sacrifice—he then recites the *yajus* mantra beginning with "iḍā devahūḥ"; this recitation is designated by the term *iḍājapa*.

Then, standing to the north of the Āhavanīya fire, he touches his hands with a mantra; this act of touching the hands is called *pāṇisaṃmarśana*, performed for the sake of attentiveness of the hands and as a form of impulsion toward the rites about to be performed.

Then he strews around the Āhavanīya, Dakṣiṇāgni, and Gārhapatya fires in order with Darbha grass. Because of the statement that "the strewing around [is performed] with sixteen Darbha blades for Agni in the directions starting from the east," the ritual act of *paristaraṇa* (strewing around) consists of spreading the grass in sequence: first upon the first girdle (*mekhalā*) in the east with four Darbha blades, and likewise in the south, west, and north.

Then, having spread darbha grass for general use upon the altar in front of the *gārhapatya* fire, he places upon it the sacrificial vessels in pairs, turned face down, washed, arranged from east to west and ending toward the north; this ritual action constitutes the procedure for the placement of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*).

Then, when the Brahman has sat down in his own place and the sacrificer has chosen him with a second choice accompanied by mantras, he spreads a continuous line of *paribhojanīya* darbha grass, starting from the middle of the *gārhapatya* fire and extending to the middle of the *āhavanīya* fire, while reciting a mantra; this rite is called the "spreading of the *pṛṣṭyā*."

Having performed the *prayāja* offerings, the Adhvaryu steps northward, sprinkles the *dhruvā* with the remaining clarified butter from the *juhū*, and sprinkles the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) in order; he then sprinkles the *upabhṛt*. This is called the "sprinkling with the remnants of the *prayāja*.

The Adhvaryu takes clarified butter once into the *juhū* from the *dhruvā* using the *sruva* spoon, issues the command to the Hotṛ with the mantra ending in "recite the invitatory verse" (*anubrūhi*) for the purpose of reciting that verse, and then takes it three times. This is called the "fourfold portion" (*caturavatta*).
He alone for whom this [five-fold cutting] occurs becomes a sacrificer who performs the four-fold cutting (*caturavattin*).

According to the statement: "The Jāmadagnyas, Vatsas, Vidās, Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, as well as the Bhārgavas, Cyāvanas, and Aurvas are declared to be performers of the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvattinaḥ*)," for sacrificers belonging to the lineages mentioned in this text, one cuts five times; this is called the *pañcāvatta*.
And the sacrificer becomes one who takes five portions (*pañcāvattin*).

Since the root *do* is recorded in the sense of "cutting apart" (*avakhaṇḍane*), the term *avadāna* refers to the cutting off of a portion from the established oblation for the purpose of taking a part measured for the *homa*.

In this manner, having taken portions and stepped across, he offers the Āgneya-ājyabhāga (the butter-portion for Agni) in the northeastern part of the Āhavanīya fire with the *sruva* ladle facing south; then, stepping back toward the north and taking portions as before, he steps across again and offers the Saumya-ājyabhāga (the butter-portion for Soma) in the southeastern region with the *sruva* ladle facing north. In that context, the two deities Agni and Soma are the referents of the term "Ājyabhāga," based on the etymological derivation: "those two for whom the *ājya* (butter) is the *bhāga* (portion)."

Immediately after the *ājyabhāga* offerings, having spread a base of clarified butter (*upastīrya*) in the *juhū* ladle, one should present the oblation (*havis*)—consisting of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth—with the mantra and a salutation with the right hand. Then, sitting down, one should touch the oblation with the mantra. Taking a portion from the eastern half of the first sacrificial cake and so forth using all five fingers—or, according to some, using the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger—one should take the portion; however, for substances such as ground flour (*caru*), one should take it only with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*). Having taken a second portion from the western half, those who follow the "five-fold cutting" (*pañcāvattin*) should take three portions: from the middle, the eastern half, and the western half.

One sprinkles [the offering] with clarified butter; the cutting of portions from the cooked rice (caru), the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and so forth, performed in this manner, is called "cutting" (avattam).

Having sprinkled the cut sacrificial oblation with clarified butter from the butter-pot while reciting a mantra, one causes the places where the portions were cut to swell; this is called "anointing back" (pratyañjanam).

Having cut [the portions] in this manner and stepped across, he offers the principal oblations (pradhānāhuti) either facing east or facing north when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered; this is called the principal sacrifice (*pradhānayāga*).

In the principal sacrifice, immediately after the cutting of the portions (avadāna) and before the crossing over (atyākramaṇa), one offers a single oblation silently with the *dhruvā* ladle using the *sruva* spoon at each respective location where the principal oblations are to be performed and at the location for the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation; this is called the "fore-offering" (*purastād-āhuti*).
Thus, immediately after the stepping back, he offers another oblation over the oblation that has been thrown; this is called the "subsequent oblation" (upariṣṭād-āhuti).

After the principal oblations, having spread an underlayer of ghee, one makes a single portion from the northern half of each of the sacrificial offerings; however, for one who follows the five-fold division, there is a double portion. Having thus made the portions, he pours ghee over them twice. When the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has been made, he offers with the *sruva* ladle an oblation to the deities of the New Moon (*darśa*) on the new moon day, and to the deities of the Full Moon (*paurṇamāsa*) on the full moon day; this is called the *pārvaṇa-homa*.

In this case, there is no approaching or touching of the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings, nor is there any re-anointing of the portions from which the cuttings were taken; having thus made the cuttings and stepped across, one offers them into the fire in the northeast quarter upon the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, and this is called the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation.

From the *ājyabhāga* offerings up to the *sviṣṭakṛt*, the Hotṛ, having uttered the *āgūra* at the recitation of the *yājyā*, pronounces the name of the deity in the accusative case using *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination), and then recites the *yājyā* with *saṃhitā*. This utterance of the deity's name is called "the designation of the deity" (*devatādeśa*).

Having heard the command "Sacrifice to Sviṣṭakṛt," having uttered the *āgura*, having designated the deity, and having recited the *nigada*, he recites the verse known as the *yājyā*; this is called the *sviṣṭakṛt-nigada*.

After the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, the *adhvaryu* steps back, offers the subsequent oblation, takes water in the *juhū* ladle, rinses it, and pours that water with a mantra toward the north in the space between the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*) and the fire; this is called the "pouring within the enclosing-sticks" (*antaḥ-paridhi-ninaya*).

Then, having washed the *juhū* ladle with water, heated it over the fire, and filled it again, he pours out the water outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) with the mantra as before; this is called the "pouring out outside the enclosing sticks" (*bahiḥ-paridhi-ninayana*).

Then, having placed the clarified butter found in the *upabhṛt* into the *juhū*, and having set both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt* back in their respective places, he portions off the *prāśitra*—belonging to the substance used in the first principal offering—into the *prāśitraharaṇa* vessel with the mantra; having sprinkled it with the handle of the *sruva* ladle, he sets it down to the west of the *praṇītā* waters. This is the portion of the *prāśitr* (the partaker); it is designated by the term *prāśitra* through the analysis of the compound as "this is for the *brahman* who eats (*prāśitr*) it."

Then, having placed the *iḍā*-vessel on the altar with its tip pointing north, one should spread a base-layer (*upastaraṇa*) of clarified butter from the *ājya*-pot into it— once for as many principal substances as there are, in a manner directed toward the north— and then [proceed with] the definition of the items to be heated.

"Thou art Virāj, the slayer of rivals; thou art Samrāj, the slayer of enemies; thou art Svarāj, the slayer of the malicious; thou art Viśvarāj, the slayer of all destructive spirits. Thus [he says]. The mantra is repeated for each instance. He sprinkles the *uparava* holes in succession with: "I sprinkle those belonging to Viṣṇu, the slayers of Rakṣas, the destroyers of secret spells (*valaga*). With this mantra repeated, he sprinkles them all. [He then] pours [water] down [into the holes] with: "The slayers of Rakṣas, the destroyers of secret spells, I pour down those belonging to Viṣṇu. Thus.

In the same manner, he pours water over all [the pits] with the mantra: "Thou art barley; keep away from us hatred, keep away enemies. Thus, he scatters barley-grains into all of them in succession. With the mantra: "I strew the slayers of Rakṣas, the slayers of Valaga, belonging to Viṣṇu," he strews sacrificial grass (*barhis*) over all the *uparavas*. With the mantra: "The slayers of Rakṣas, the slayers of Valaga, I offer upon [them], belonging to Viṣṇu, Svāhā!"—having placed gold upon each of the *uparavas*, he offers oblations with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) over them in succession.
The sacrificer says, "This for the Vaiṣṇava uparavas. This is called the consecration of the uparavas.

Having taken up the two *adhiṣavaṇa* pressing-boards, each measuring one and a half *prādeśas* in width and three *prādeśas* in length, which together form a square; he places them joined together over those *uparavas* with the formula: "I place you, the two Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu. To prevent them from slipping, he fixes them on the front side with two pegs, on the back with two, and on both sides with two. Thus, having fixed them with six pegs, [he proceeds].

"I strew around the two Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-destroyers, belonging to Viṣṇu. He strews around with loose earth in a clockwise direction. "I spread around the two Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-destroyers, belonging to Viṣṇu. With these words, he spreads sacrificial grass over those two. "The two Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-destroyers, belonging to Viṣṇu. With this, he touches them. This much of the ritual action is called the installation of the wooden slabs upon the sounding-holes (*uparava*).

Then, with the mantra "tato yajñapratiṣṭhā" or silently, having spread an ox-hide over the two boards, he causes the pressing-stones to sound upon the boards across the hide with the formula: "Thou art great, a great stone; utter a great voice for Indra. He places the skin in the seat (nīḍa) with the formula: "O stones, [place] the good stone. This concludes the explanation of the ritual items according to the Śrauta tradition at the front of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.

He binds handfuls of *barhis* grass for the purpose of preparing the hymns of praise. Then, having addressed the sacrificer with "Come, O Sacrificer," he digs up the middle of the *āgnīdhrīya* mound with the wooden sword (*sphya*), sprinkles it with water, and having scattered the earth and sand from the *cātvāla* pit thereupon, he fashions a circular mound (*khara*) one cubit in measure. Both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer recite the mantra: "Thou art pervasive, the carrier; protect me with thy fierce aspect, O Agni; nourish me, do not harm me. This is called the preparation of the *āgnīdhrīya* mound.

Inside the *sadas*, leaving two steps toward the east, he prepares the *hotṛ-khara* on the *pṛṣṭhyā* line in the same manner [as the others], with the formula: "Thou art Vahni, the bearer of oblations; do not harm us with the Raudra [weapon]! This *hotṛ-khara* is called the *hotṛ-dhiṣṇya*.

Having carried [the fire] around in front of the Āhavanīya, he prepares the mound for the Maitrāvaruṇa at a distance of one cubit to the south of the Hotṛ’s Dhiṣṇya, saying: "Thou art Śvātra, the wise; thou belongest to Rudra. This mound is called the Maitrāvaruṇa-dhiṣṇya.

One *aratni* to the north of that *dhiṣṇya* is that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin: "Thou art Tutha, the all-knowing; thou art with the Raudra [deity]. This mound is called the *dhiṣṇya* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.

To the north of that, at a distance of one aratni, he prepares the mound for the Potṛ priest with the formula: "Thou art the eager one, the sage; thou hast sat down with the Raudra [oblation]. This mound is called the Potṛkhara.

To the north of that, at a distance of one cubit (aratni), the Neṣṭṛ prepares the sounding-place (khara) with the formula: "Thou art Aṅghāri, thou art Bambhāri; thou hast been [prepared] by Raudra. This sounding-place of the Neṣṭṛ is called his dhiṣṇya.

At a distance of one *aratni* to the north of that is the place for the *acchāvāka*. With the mantra, "Thou art the seeker of aid, the worshipper; thou art with the Raudra [deity]," this *khara* is called the *acchāvāka-dhiṣṇya*.

On the *mārjālīya* [fire-altar], he prepares the *khara* [elevated mound] as on the *āgnīdhrīya*. "Thou art pure; thou hast been cleansed by the Raudra [formula]"—this *khara* is called the *mārjālīya-dhiṣṇya*. This is the etymological explanation of the ritual term.

He silently pours the remaining earth and sand from the *cātvāla* into the *āgnīdhrīya* fire-pit. Then the Adhvaryu pays homage to the fire on the northern altar (*auttaravedika*), saying: "Thou art the sovereign (*samrāj*), the consumer of grass; thou hast been won by Raudra. Then he pays homage to the *āstāva*, saying: "Thou art the one to be sat around (*pariṣadya*), the purifier (*pavamāna*); thou hast been won by Raudra. Then [he pays homage] to the *cātvāla*, saying: "Thou art the runner (*pratakvā*), the windy one (*nabhasvant*); thou hast been won by Raudra. Then he pays homage to the animal-cooking fire (*paśuśrapaṇa*), saying: "Thou art the uncleaned (*asammṛṣṭa*), the preparer of oblations (*havyasūda*); thou hast been won by Raudra."

Standing at the western door of the assembly hall (*sadas*), he worships the *audumbarī* post with the mantra: "Thou art the abode of Truth (*ṛtadhāman*), the light of heaven; thou hast been won by Raudra. Then he worships the seat of the Brahman priest (*brahmasadana*) with the mantra: "Thou art the light of Brahman (*brahmajyotis*), the abode of heaven; thou hast been won by Raudra. Remaining in that very place, he worships the *śālāmukhīya* fire with the mantra: "Thou art Aja Ekapād, the one-footed; thou hast been won by Raudra. Then he worships the *gārhapatya* fire with the mantra: "Thou art the serpent of the depths (*budhniya*); thou hast been won by Raudra. This is called the worship beginning from the northern altar (*auttaravedika*).

From this point on, the Adhvaryu shall not pass beyond the Sadas toward the west; remaining right there, he issues the directions: "Strew the sacrificial grass! Give the command! Call those who share in the vow! Strew the Āstāva thickly! O Unnetṛ, having placed the two *daśāpavitra* strainers into the *droṇakalaśa*, place the pressing-stones and the Vāyu-vessels [there]. Place the wife in the wife’s hall! O Agnīdh, heat the clarified butter! O Pratiprasthātṛ, cleanse the offering-spoons! Bring the butter for the *pṛṣadājya*! Fetch the curds!
This direction is called the direction for the strewing of the sacrificial grass and so forth at the Great Altar (*mahāvedi*).

At the southern edge of the altar, he spreads a handful of large sacrificial grass (*mahābarhis*) with the original formula: "O divine grass, may you be soft as wool. He spreads the large altar extensively toward the east and facing westward. Silently, he hands over the vow-food consisting of half a breast. The Unnetṛ [prepares] five or seventeen pressing-stones (*grāvan*), made of *vāyavya* wood, a span in length, shaped like mortars, and single-faced; ten cups (*camasa*), a pouring-vessel (*pariplu-pātra*), and the rest—this is the definition of the ritual items according to the Śrauta tradition.

Having washed the *raha* shaped like a ladle, the *droṇakalaśa*, the two *daśāpavitra* strainers, the four jars, the *upagraha* vessels, and whatever else has been used, and having placed all these together with the *daśāpavitra* strainers into the *droṇakalaśa*, he sets them all down in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall. Among the Vāyavya cups, that which is made of Udumbara wood and is four-cornered is called the *dadhi-graha* vessel.
The vessel marked with a girdle (*rāsnā*) is called the Aindravāyava vessel. The vessel marked with a *pilaka* (protuberance) is called the Maitrāvaruṇa vessel.
The two-cornered vessel is called the Āśvina cup;
the vessel made of Bilva wood is called the Śukra cup;
and the smooth vessel made of Vikaṅkata wood is called the Manthin cup.
It is made of smooth udumbara wood and is designated as "unassailable" (adābhya).
Vessels fashioned from *nyagrodha* wood are called *atigrāhya*.
There are two bowls with openings on both sides, designated as the *ṛtupātra*.
The other vessels are made either of *nyagrodha* or *udumbara* wood. The *camasa* cups are made of *nyagrodha* wood. A square cup with few flaws is called the *brahmacamasa*.
That staff which is circular in shape is called the Hotṛ’s cup;
that staff which has a broad top becomes the Sacrificer’s cup.
That which is triangular with a handle is designated as the *udgātṛ* cup;
that which is curved at the bottom with a handle is called the *praśāstṛ* cup;
and that which is curved at the top with a handle is the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* cup.
In the same manner, that staff provided with a girth-band becomes the cup for the Acchāvāka;
that sharp-pointed staff becomes the cup for the Āgnīdhra.

The Adhvaryu prepares the strainer from the branch of the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma according to the ritual for the animal sacrifice. Then he places the animal cooking-pot, the branch-strainer, the two omentum-spits, the two ropes, the spit, and the staff for the Maitrāvaruṇa upon the Darbha grass to the north of the Śālāmukhīya fire.
The Definition of Śrauta Ritual Terms.

He sprinkles [the vessels] with the archetypal mantra, "Be purified" (*śundhadhvam*). The Āgnīdhra, having rubbed his hands together, kindled the fires, strewn them around, and spread *darbha* grass in front of the *Śālāmukhīya* fire, places upon it the ritual implements—the wooden sword (*sphya*), the *agnihotrahavaṇī*, the *juhū*, and so forth—just as in the animal sacrifice. The Pratiprasthātṛ melts the clarified butter (*ājya*) over the Gārhapatya fire. Having performed the rubbing of his hands and seated the Brahman priest to the south, he spreads the *pṛṣṭhyā* line from the *Śālāmukhīya* fire to the *Uttaravedi* altar, and [prepares] the two strainers (*pavitra*).

Having performed [the preliminary rites], he gives the command to the sacrificer, "Restrain your speech. Having addressed the sacrificer thus, he takes up the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle with the standard mantra, heats it over the fire in the same manner as before, performs the consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* waters, and sprinkles the vessels with the standard mantra. He pours out both the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the curd (*dadhi*) in the same manner, places them on the fire, and carries fire around both. Then the Adhvaryu, having rubbed his hands together and performed the taking up of the wooden sword (*sphya*) and other rites with the standard mantra, fixes the *sphya* at the place of the *khara* mound and issues the formal command (*sampraiṣa*).

"Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters," and so forth, as in the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*). The *āgnīdhra* places the *prokṣaṇī* waters down. The *adhvaryu* hands over the wooden sword (*sphya*) as in the archetype. The *pratiprasthātṛ* places the fuel (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) near the northern altar (*uttaravedi*). The *āgnīdhra*, taking the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) in his right hand and the under-layer (*upastaraṇa*) and tips of the *vedī* grass in his left, heats them over the *śālāmukhīya* fire with the mantra "O you two, [I purify] the fire. Having wiped both with the same mantra used for the *sruva*, he hands them to the *pratiprasthātṛ*.

The Pratiprasthātṛ, having heated the *juhū* and other vessels like those used for the animal sacrifice and wiped them clean, throws the tips of the *vedī* grass into the *Śālāmukhīya* fire. Having placed the vessels on the grass in front of the *utkara*, he takes them up again and sets them down near the *Śālāmukhīya*. The wife, having looked at the *Śālāmukhīya* fire and the clarified butter (*ājya*), causes the sacrificer to look at the clarified butter.

The *adhvaryu* brings the *prokṣaṇī* waters to the north, personally inspects the clarified butter (*ājya*), purifies it, and having purified the *prokṣaṇī* waters as well, takes the *ājya* and the curd. Accompanied by the *brahman* and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), he goes to the *prāgvaṃśa* hall; having taken the portions of clarified butter for the ladles upon the altar according to the ritual of the animal sacrifice, and having handed them over to the assistants, he touches water and gives King Soma to the *brahman*. The *brahman*, taking King Soma, encloses the area in front of the *śālāmukhīya* fire, stands to the north, and leads him following after the fire. [This concludes] the definition of the ritual items according to the *Śrauta* tradition.

The Adhvaryu, having placed the fuel for the leading forward [of the fire] upon the Śālāmukhīya fire and having prepared the supporting ladles from the Cātvāla pit, melts clarified butter over the ancient Gārhapatya fire and purifies it. Then, while the sacrificer, his wife, his sons, his grandsons, and his kinsmen hold on to one another in order of seniority, the Adhvaryu takes four portions of butter in the *pracaraṇī* ladle and offers it into the Śālāmukhīya fire.

"O Soma, you are the wide-extended protector against those who harm our bodies, against those who act with hostility, and against those who do us wrong; Svāhā! The sacrificer says, "To Soma, this [offering]. Then he offers with the *sruva* ladle: "May the swift one, enjoying the clarified butter, accept it; Svāhā! The sacrificer says, "To Agni, this [offering]. Having again taken four portions, he issues the formal command (*saṃpraiṣa*): "Recite for Agni and Soma as they are being led forward. This is called the *saṃpraiṣa* for the leading forward of Agni and Soma.

When the first *hotṛ* verse has been recited three times, they lift the fuel from the *śālāmukhīya* fire and go out by the eastern door. The King [Soma] follows, as do the clarified butter offerings; the pressing stones and the *vāyavya* cups follow after. [They proceed] with the mantra: "May this Agni create wide space for us; may he go before us, shattering our adversaries. May he, exulting, conquer the enemies; may he win the prize in the struggle for booty."

Then, having gone around the north of the *sadas*, having placed the fire in the *āgnīdhra* shed, having strewn grass around it and poured water around it, he makes an oblation with four ladlings: "O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God, knowing all ways; keep away from us the crooked sin; we shall offer to thee the most abundant word of homage, svāhā! Thus [he offers]. "To Agni this [belongs]," says the sacrificer. Right here, having set down the pressing-stones and the *vāyavya* cups, and having gone past the *āgnīdhrīya* hearth along with the King Soma and the others...

He offers a spoonful (sruvāhuti) into the Āhavanīya fire with the mantra: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely, svāhā! The sacrificer [dedicates] this to Viṣṇu. The Brahman priest, having handed over the King Soma to another, sits down with the mantra; the sacrificer also sits in his own place. The Adhvaryu, while pouring out the sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇī), performs the rites beginning with that and ending with "Whatever [fault] of mine, O Agni," according to the procedure for the animal sacrifice. He performs the sprinkling and other rites upon the mound (khara). This is the definition of the Śrauta ritual elements.

He pours out the sprinkling waters at the western corner of the great altar (*mahāvedi*). The Brahman priest returns as he came and takes up the King Soma. The sacrificer also, having touched water, returns by the same way he went, takes the King from the presence of the Brahman, and causes him to enter the *havirdhāna* shed by the eastern door with the mantra: "May Soma, the knower of the path, go to the gods; he goes to his appointed place to sit in the womb of Truth. The Adhvaryu, having touched water, spreads a black antelope skin in the interior of the southern *havirdhāna* shed with the mantra: "Thou art the seat of Aditi."

The sacrificer places the King (Soma) upon that black antelope skin with the formula: "Sit on the seat of Aditi. With the formula, "O divine Savitṛ, this is your Soma; guard him; let them not deceive you," he hands over the King to the deities. He worships that Soma with the formula: "O divine Soma, as a god you have approached the gods; here I, a man, approach men, together with offspring and with abundance of wealth. With the words, "Homage to the gods," he makes a reverential salutation with his joined palms extended eastward over the Soma.

With the formula, "Svadhā to the ancestors," he makes a downward-extended añjali gesture to the south of that [fire]. Having touched water, he steps out with the formula, "Here I am released from the noose of Varuṇa. Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "May I behold the light of Vaiśvānara, the sun. The Adhvaryu gives the command: "Release the intermediate consecration (avāntaradīkṣā). Thereupon, the sacrificer [acts].

"O Agni, Lord of Vows, you are the lord of vows among vows. That body of mine which was in you, let that be here in me; that body of yours which was in me, let that be there in you. O Lord of Vows, according to our respective natures, let the vows of us two who observe the vow be fulfilled. With these words, he worships the Āhavanīya fire. [The Adhvaryu:]

"O sacrificer, loosen the girdle from the wives; let them call out your name, mentioning your ancestors—your fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, as well as your sons and grandsons—and let the Subrahmaṇya priest invoke the Subrahmaṇyā. Thus he gives the command. At the conclusion of the omentum offering (*vapā-yāga*), the Subrahmaṇya priest performs the invocation for the father's son. He does this either at the end of the sacrificial post-pit (*yūpāvaṭa*) rite or immediately now. Then he requests [the materials], beginning with "containing barley," and so forth; the rites from the washing of the sacrificial post up to the wiping of the omentum are performed as in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*).
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *Nirūḍhapaśu* sacrifice, wherever there is the term "Indra-Agni," [that is modified].

The Definition of Śrauta Ritual Terms: In this context, the specific modification (*ūha*) to be made is for the term *agnīṣoma*. When the *pitāputrīyā* has been invoked, he takes a firm jar, goes out northward between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, stands facing the stream at the junction of shade and sunlight, and draws the waters known as the *vasatīvarī*: "These waters are full of oblation; the divine sacrifice is full of oblation; he desires to win it with oblation; may Sūrya be full of oblation. If the sun has already set, he draws the water after interposing gold.
He takes [the water] in the shade of the sun, in the shade of his own body, or in the shade of a tree; this is called the taking of the *vasatīvarī* waters.

Then, having turned clockwise and placed the *vasatīvarī* pitcher in his left hand, he goes between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, passes north of the *āgnīdhrīya* shed and the *sadas*, enters the hall through the eastern door, and sets them down together behind the *śālāmukhīya* fire with the formula: "I set you down in the seat of Agni, whose house is secure; for the sake of bliss, O blissful ones, bestow bliss upon me. This is called the setting down of the *vasatīvarī* waters.

Then, beginning with "The fires, the sacrificial cake," and so forth, the procedure is like that of the animal sacrifice, excluding the *svaru*-offering and ending with the *ājyeḍā*. The specific difference is the carrying away of the embers for the *aupayāja* offerings from the *āgnīdhrīya* fire. At the offering of the sacrificial cake, the sacrificer's consecration formula is "May I become a slayer of Vṛtra"; at the offering of the limbs, it is "May I become possessed of sensory power. At the end of the cleansing after the *ājyeḍā*, having offered over the mortar and pestle with the formula "In the mortar, in the pestle," and having replenished the *dhruvā* ladle, he performs the expiatory offerings (*prāyaścitta*), or not.
The ritual action beginning from "Now the one belonging to Agni-Soma" up to this point is designated as the *agnīṣomīya-paśu* (the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni-Soma).

Having washed the heart-spit (*hṛdayaśūla*) and set it aside, he issues the command: "Depart; do not sit around me. This is called the command for going outside the altar (*bahirvedibhavana-praiṣa*). Then they all go outside the altar. Taking the *vasatīvarī* waters, having led them along the path behind the Gārhapatya fire, and having gone out by the southern door—this is the definition of the ritual act according to the Śrauta texts.

Having placed [the ladle] on his left shoulder and having carried it around the Mārjālīya fire and the Sadas with his right hand, he sets it down to the south, touching the sacrificial post, facing northward, with the formula: "You are the portion of Indra and Agni. Having taken it up again, turned back toward the north, and placed it on his left shoulder, he returns by the same way he came and sets it down behind the Śālāmukhīya fire, touching it, with the formula: "You are the portion of Mitra and Varuṇa."

Taking them up again, placing them on his right shoulder, and having gone out by the eastern door, he goes around the north of the *sadas* and the *āgnīdhra*, and sets them down in contact with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) from the north, saying: "You are the portion of all the gods. Taking them up again, turning clockwise, placing them on his left shoulder, and returning by that same path, he sets them down in contact behind the *niṣṇaya* of the *āgnīdhra* fire, saying: "Be watchful at the sacrifice. This is called the setting down of the *vasatīvarī* waters.

Then he issues the directions: "Prepare curds for the *dadhigharma* from the cow that milks for the Sovereign; prepare the *āmikṣā* from the cow that belongs to the sacrificer; prepare milk and parched barley-meal for the *āśira* from the cow that belongs to the wife; prepare curds for the *śṛtātaṅkya* and for the *ādityagraha*; prepare the flour for the sacrificial cakes; prepare the parched grains for the *hāriyojana* cup; prepare four *udabhraṇas*, three *udañcanas*, an odd number of *ekadhana* jars—the lowest being three and the highest eleven—two ropes, and two omentum-spits."

"Make the fuel and the sacrificial grass into one mass, prepare the large enclosing sticks from *udumbara* wood, and let the *subrahmaṇyā* be invoked. This is called the injunction for the preparation of the materials for the *sutyā*.

One of the Adhvaryu’s assistants, having cut the leaves from the branches in sequence—leaving those intended for the *savanīya* offerings—having placed them in front of the *śālāmukhīya* fire, having stripped the bases to make *upaveṣas*, and having set them down to the west of the *śālāmukhīya* in a known manner; having prepared the second and last *śākhāpavitra* with the original mantra and the other six *śākhāpavitra*s silently; and having placed six milking vessels, six *śākhāpavitra*s, and eight pots to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire.

Having sprinkled [the milk] with the common mantra, having drawn out the embers with the respective fire-stirring sticks (*upaveṣa*), having placed the respective strainers (*pavitra*) [upon them], having caused it to be milked with the respective milking vessel, and having heated it, he should take it down toward the north.
